chapter_theme: The Buddha debate opens: Neelakesi travels to the Buddha's city, finds flesh sold in its market and argues that the buyer and eater share the killing, mocking the Buddha's compassion for leaving flesh unforbidden; she then finds the Buddha teaching the three scriptures and the aggregates, charges his doctrines with contradiction, and makes him set out the aggregates, which he begins to expound down to the octads of form and the four elements.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha, whom Neelakesi debates in person in his city; also called சுகதன், சேடன், தோன்றல்
the people standing in the Buddha's town whom Neelakesi addresses about the meat market
the followers who sit worshipping the Buddha and hear his teaching (தமர்கள், 479)

463.reading: Naming the fair lands, the rivers, the lands of sickness, the great burning grounds and the jewelled mountains as she passes them, Neelakesi reaches the beautiful city of Sugata, the Buddha.
463.nuance: The journey is told as her own pointing speech (இவைதாம் repeated), so the land is seen through the traveller's eyes; சுகதன் (line 4) names the Buddha by the title Sugata, which marks the town as his own.
463.event: Neelakesi travels through lands, rivers, forests and mountains and arrives at the Buddha's city.

464.reading: Amid the sound of drums and the ringing of bells, someone says that this, greater than its walls, is the place where the lord of the red-robed ones dwells.
464.nuance: The verse has only three lines and the speaker of எனலும் is not named; whether it is Neelakesi herself or someone on the road who points out the town cannot be fixed. செம்படர்கள் (line 2) seems to name the ochre-robed monks, but the sense of சிறையின் மிகுமால் is unclear.
464.event: Someone points out the Buddha's dwelling place as Neelakesi approaches.

465.reading: The description of the city goes on: buildings like rain-clouded mountains, flags on bamboo poles, groves of plantain, and men wearing garlands and women with spread tresses who, if one must name them, are tigers of the caves and peacocks.

466.reading: The catalogue of the land continues with the coast: fishing boats riding the tall white waves, swift ships moving, groves loud with bees, and fair ponds, mounds and sandy jungle tracts.
466.nuance: The verse has no main verb; its list runs on into 467, where எனவும் closes it.

467.reading: It is said too to be a land of rich fields where kayal fish leap and water lilies open, and a land adorned in ways the following lines describe obscurely.
467.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (முயன்மீ னெறியு முறியுங் கறியா தயன்மே யுறையா தணியிற்று) resist parsing; they seem to praise the land's order or plenty, but no single sense can be fixed.

468.reading: It is said also to hold a burning ground where flocks of vultures and demons gather, shrouded corpses lie, fat and bodies mingle, and bones are heaped up.
468.nuance: The burning ground stands in the same list as the coast and the fields, without comment; in a work whose heroine was a demon of the burning ground (the opening sarukkams), the place is part of the ordinary landscape rather than a horror.

469.reading: Neelakesi says that the very street shows what became of the scriptures that taught the cruel sorrow of wandering through births, and those standing there answer that the Buddhists here do not condemn flesh.
469.nuance: The verse turns on the reading of ஆனின்றாரும் (line 3) as 'those standing there', which makes line 4 a bystanders' report; it could also be Neelakesi's own sarcasm. The charge that flesh-eating is allowed is answered at once in 470 to 474.
469.event: In the Buddha's town Neelakesi remarks on the street, and bystanders tell her the Buddhists there do not condemn meat.

claims.claim: the Buddhist scriptures teach the great sorrow of wandering through births
eating flesh bought in the market is not blameworthy

470.reading: Neelakesi asks the bystanders whether they will not call it evil for the robed ones who preached dharma to eat flesh from the market, when creatures living all around have come there as meat.
470.nuance: The robe is described lavishly (dyed like marutham flowers where bees hum), so the finery of the dress is set against the stall of meat; the charge is about the gap between preaching dharma and buying flesh, not only about diet.

claims.claim: those who preach dharma yet eat flesh bought in the market do evil, since the creatures were killed for that market

471.reading: Neelakesi points to the animals in the market, which seem to lift their heads and open their mouths to say that because buyers with money want flesh the netters lay down their lives for that price, so is the killer alone the cruel one?
471.nuance: The argument is given to the victims: the slaughtered beasts themselves seem to blame the buyer, which turns an economic argument (price draws the net) into an accusation spoken by the dead.

claims.claim: the buyers' demand for flesh is what makes the hunter kill, so the killer is not the only culprit

472.reading: Neelakesi says that the teacher who gave away his own wife and laboured only for others, wanting nothing for himself, had only to say that the one who eats flesh also gathers evil karma, and the many animals on earth would have lived without dying.
472.nuance: The Buddha's legendary self-giving (the gift of his wife, a former-birth story) is granted in full, and then used against him: his compassion stopped short of the one word that would have saved the animals. The praise is the weapon.

claims.claim: the Buddha in a former life gave away his own wife and toiled only for others
the one who eats flesh, not only the one who kills, incurs evil karma

473.reading: With irony Neelakesi calls the Buddha a knower who would not speak without reflection, and says this too is his kindness, that he will lift all, together with his own children, into the burning hell: truly a most gracious and noble one.
473.nuance: Every term of praise (பெரிதாம் அளியன், பெருந்தகையன்) is meant in reverse; the verse says the teacher's permission of flesh is a fault of knowledge, not a lapse, since he 'knew rightly'.

claims.claim: a teacher who permits flesh-eating leads himself and his disciples into the fiery hell

474.reading: Neelakesi says that, like a middleman who neither sells nor buys outright but takes his profit between them, the umbrella-bearing monk who piles up foul meat, recites his threefold excuse and goes off covered in his robe is a very Death to living beings.
474.nuance: முத்துரைத்து (line 3), 'speaking three', is read here as the threefold test by which meat is pure for a monk (not seen, heard or suspected to be killed for him); that reading is likely but not certain from the verse. The simile matters: the middleman profits from a trade he does not perform, as the eater profits from a killing he does not do.

claims.claim: meat is pure for a monk when three conditions show it was not killed for him
the eater who neither kills nor sells still shares the killing, like a middleman who profits from both sides

475.reading: Saying 'let us go and see the master who, like one who comes up beside dancers and watchers and spins out matching words, sorts out who incurs sin and who does not, the killer or the eater', Neelakesi goes on.
475.nuance: The teacher is mocked as a talker who fits his words to whoever is listening; the claim she means to test, that the sin is the killer's and not the eater's, has already been answered in 471 and 474.
475.event: Neelakesi resolves to go and confront the Buddha himself and sets out.

claims.claim: the sin of killing falls on the one who killed, not on the one who eats

476.reading: Under the shade of the fair peepal the handsome teacher sits on a flowered seat that sheds the rays of many gems; some praise and worship him, saying he has shown resolve, but he sits wrapped in his robe, moved by nothing.
476.nuance: பரிவிலன் (line 4) can be read as calm detachment or as coldness to his worshippers; the narrator does not say which, and the robe 'buried' around him (படம் புதைத்து) keeps the picture ambiguous.
476.event: Devotees worship the Buddha seated under the peepal tree, and he sits unmoved.

477.reading: To those who sit there sure that he is the trustworthy teacher, the noble one divides his doctrine's meaning many ways, saying this is the Sutra, this the Vinaya, this the other, the Shastra, these three.
477.event: The Buddha expounds his teaching to the assembled devotees.

claims.claim: the teaching is set out in three scriptures, the Sutra, the Vinaya and the Shastra

478.reading: He goes on to declare that the five aggregates are momentary, that there is nothing that knows having first examined, and yet joins by reasoning that there is a person (pudgala), and also that apart from what cannot be spoken there is nothing.
478.nuance: The verse is built to show the doctrines at odds: momentary aggregates and no lasting knower set against a person that is somehow there. Line 4 (மந்திலாற் சொலாப் பாட்டினோடு) is obscure; 'the unsayable' is read from 480's அவாச்சியம். This is the Jain poet's account of Buddhist teaching; a person held to be inexpressible belongs to one Buddhist school, not to all. The claims are answered in 479 to 482.

claims.claim: the five aggregates are momentary
there is no knower that persists from one moment to the next
there is nonetheless a person (pudgala)

479.reading: The dark-haired one comes up to the Buddha as he tells his followers that these are the true principles, and says: you babbled many things like a madman, and I will show that what you babbled agrees in no way.
479.event: Neelakesi approaches the Buddha and challenges his teaching.

claims.claim: the Buddha's doctrines contradict one another in every way

480.reading: Neelakesi lists the contradictions: he says the five aggregates exist, yet expounds that form with feeling, perception and formation does not exist; he joins a person by reasoning; and he speaks of nothingness and of the inexpressible besides.
480.nuance: Line 3 repeats 478's line 3 almost word for word but with போதியால் for புந்தியால்; one is likely a copyist's slip.

claims.claim: one cannot hold both that the aggregates exist and that form, feeling, perception and formation do not
there is a person (pudgala) besides the aggregates

481.reading: The Buddha answers that even if many of the things he said of the five do not fit, there is a point in the reality of the aggregates, so the mental states too exist and she should be clear on it; Neelakesi laughs and asks whether he is the one who preached dharma to Nanda.
481.nuance: The Buddha concedes ground (அமைவில எனினும்) before he holds it, which the poet means as a first retreat. Neelakesi's laugh names Nanda, the Buddha's kinsman whom tradition says he converted, as if to ask how such a muddled teacher won anyone.
481.event: The Buddha partly concedes and defends the reality of the aggregates; Neelakesi laughs at him.

claims.claim: though some of its divisions fail, the aggregates are real and so the mental states exist

482.reading: Neelakesi says that he has spoken many tenets of his choosing, and if all but one were lost and he claimed goodness from that one, it would be like a man covered head to foot in leprosy who touches only his clean tuft of hair: is he pure?
482.nuance: The simile answers 481's concession: one sound tenet cannot clean a doctrine that is sick everywhere else.

claims.claim: one sound tenet does not make a doctrine sound when the rest of it is faulty

483.reading: Neelakesi tells him to set out the five aggregates he established as good, and she will make clear that they are not; the elder in the ochre robe then begins slowly to expound them, bidding her listen.
483.event: Neelakesi challenges the Buddha to state the aggregates, and he begins to expound them.

claims.claim: the five aggregates as the Buddha teaches them do not exist

484.reading: The Buddha lists the aggregates with their divisions: form; feeling of three kinds; consciousness of six; perception in like number; and formation of twenty in two kinds; these, he says, are our wealth.
484.nuance: The counts (three feelings, six consciousnesses, twenty formations) are read from compressed lines and line 2 (மருவா தனமாண் குறியத் துணைசெய்) is hard to divide. The list is finer than the bare five names of the Manimekalai; it is answered from 494, where Neelakesi vows to burn the aggregates like a hunter's hut.

claims.claim: the aggregates are form, three kinds of feeling, six kinds of consciousness, perception and twenty formations

485.reading: The Buddha tells her, fair-browed one with fragrant garland, that of the five in order the first, form, contains within its bounds many octads, each fixed as eight joined together.
485.nuance: The octad (அட்டகம்) is the smallest unit of matter as eight inseparable things together; 495 answers it, arguing that if the mass is inseparable its parts become mere qualities of one bearer, or else must be separate things.

claims.claim: material form is made of octads, units of eight things joined inseparably

486.reading: He names the eight: earth, water, fire and wind, with colour, taste, fine smell and touch; and says that what is left out of the eight can be told, with sound and appearance.
486.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (இலவே யவையெட் டினும்விட் டதிறம் ...) are hard to construe; the reading that sound is added outside the eight is a guess.

claims.claim: the eight of the octad are the four elements with colour, taste, smell and touch

487.reading: He gives the marks and works of the four great elements: earth is hard, water moist, fire hot and wind brings motion; and their functions are bearing, holding together, drying and stirring.
487.nuance: Each element has a nature and a function: earth bears, water binds, fire dries or ripens, wind stirs. The reading of அயர்த்தல் as 'holding together' is from the pattern of the list.

claims.claim: the four great elements are known by hardness, moisture, heat and motion, and act by bearing, binding, drying and stirring

links.note: Kural 256 says no one would sell flesh for a price if the world did not kill to eat; 471 makes the market's beasts say the buyers' money sends the netter out to kill them.
links.teaches: The couplet's demand argument is given a voice and an opponent: in the Buddha's own town the dead animals accuse the buyer, so the rule becomes a charge against a monastic order that buys rather than kills.

gains.a: the verse's picture of the protesting beasts gets the Kural's general law of price and killing behind it
gains.b: the couplet's abstract buyer becomes a named religious community, which shows whom the argument was useful against

links.note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh to swell his own can hold to grace; 472 grants the Buddha the greatest self-giving, even of his wife, and still faults him for not forbidding flesh.
links.teaches: Grace in the Kural is lost by the eater; the Neelakesi adds a teacher's grace lost by silence, so that a life of total giving can still fail the test if it leaves others free to eat flesh.

gains.a: the charge against the Buddha gets the Kural's rule that grace and flesh-eating cannot go together
gains.b: the couplet's test is extended from the one who eats to the one who teaches and does not forbid

links.note: Kural 255 says hell does not open its mouth to release one who eats flesh; 473 says the Buddha, by permitting flesh, will lead himself and his disciples into the burning hell.
links.teaches: The Kural's hell takes the single eater; the Jain polemic widens it to a teacher and his whole following, so a permission given in doctrine becomes a collective path to hell.

gains.a: the ironic praise of the Buddha's 'kindness' gets the Kural's plain sentence on where flesh-eating leads
gains.b: the couplet's punishment is shown to reach the teacher who permits as well as the one who eats

links.note: Thirikadugam 36 names among the self-deceived the one who eats flesh and claims compassion and the one who says the deed is done without his consent; 474 answers that defence with the middleman who profits from a trade he does not perform.
links.teaches: The Thirikadugam only lists the excuse 'it was not done with my consent'; the Neelakesi gives the reason it fails, since the eater stands to the killing as a middleman to a sale, profiting from both sides.

gains.a: the attack on the monk's threefold excuse is shown to be a known type of self-deception in the ethical manuals
gains.b: the verse's bare list gets an argument and a target, the Buddhist rule of meat not killed for the eater

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 69 binds the sin of a killing on five: the killer, the one who consented, the one who took the carcass, the cook and the eater; 475 mocks a master who sorts sin so that the killer bears it and the eater does not.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show the Jain account of shared guilt as a deliberate counter-rule: the Sirupanchamoolam's five sharers are the answer to the very division of guilt the Neelakesi's Buddha is said to make.

gains.a: Neelakesi's mockery gets a full rule of who shares a killing, which the verse only implies
gains.b: the manual's list of five is shown to be aimed at a rival doctrine that confined guilt to the killer

links.note: 251 charged the monk Arkkachandran with preaching compassion while eating fish and flesh; 470 brings the same charge to the Buddha's own town and its market, before the teacher himself.
links.teaches: The flesh charge moves from the disciple's conduct to the master's city and then (472-473) to the master's teaching, so the poem traces a monk's fault back to the rule that permits it.

links.note: In 177 Kundalakesi reports that her teacher first taught the three scriptures and the five aggregates; in 477 the Buddha himself is shown dividing his teaching into Sutra, Vinaya and Shastra and then the aggregates.
links.teaches: The Neelakesi climbs from report to source: the doctrine Neelakesi first met second-hand from a nun is now spoken by the Buddha in person, so the debate that follows is staged as a refutation at the root.

links.note: In 203 Neelakesi argued that a power passing across the moments would be a sixth thing beside the five aggregates; in 478 and 480 the Buddha's teaching posits a person (pudgala) besides the aggregates.
links.teaches: The 'sixth thing' that Neelakesi forced on Kundalakesi as an absurd consequence turns up as the master's own tenet, the person, so the earlier argument becomes the charge of contradiction here.

links.note: In 194 Neelakesi argued that feeling, perception and formation are not other than knowing, so the five aggregates collapse; in 481 the Buddha concedes that many of his divisions of the five do not fit but holds the aggregates real.
links.teaches: The objection made against the disciple is half admitted by the master, which lets the poet show the Buddhist defence retreating from the five divisions to a bare claim that the aggregates exist.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher names the five aggregates simply (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness); the Neelakesi's Buddha gives them with numbered subdivisions, three feelings, six consciousnesses and twenty formations.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic gives the aggregates as a short list within the four truths; the Jain epic's Buddha gives a scholastic count, so the polemic attacks a more technical Abhidharma than the one the Buddhist epic chose to teach.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika gives earth as hard, water cool, fire burning and wind moving, borne by eternal atoms; the Neelakesi's Buddha gives the same four marks with functions, borne by octads of momentary form (478, 485).
links.teaches: Across two polemical epics the marks of the elements are common ground; what the schools dispute is the bearer, eternal unchanging atoms for the Ajivika against momentary eight-fold clusters for the Buddhist.

new_concepts.gloss: the Buddha: the awakened teacher of dharma, his coming in a dark age, and the worship of his seat and footprints
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: புத்த னார் (479); also சுகதன் (463)

new_concepts.gloss: the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) that are spoken of as a person
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: கந்த மைந்திவை (478), கந்தமைந் துளவெனி (480)

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம்); the id differs from vaadham, which the list already uses for alchemy

new_concepts.gloss: the cremation ground, with its pyres, corpses, bones and the demons and goddess held to haunt it
new_concepts.label_source: label from neelakesi 32; this verse says இடுகாடு (468)

source_issues: 464 has three lines; a line seems lost, and the speaker of எனலும் cannot be recovered.
478 line 3 reads புந்தியால் where the near-identical 480 line 3 reads போதியால்; one is probably a copyist's slip.
479 line 4 ends in என்னெவெ, apparently a garbled form of a closing word such as என்னவே or என்றலும்.
482 line 3 is divided oddly (எழுந்தவன குடுமி), probably for எழுந்தவன் குடுமி.
470 is printed with almost no word division in lines 1 to 4.
